conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS**. It’s simply a well-researched set of questions that helps us understand how moms are feeling emotionally in the weeks after birth, so we can make sure you’re getting the right support.

Everything we discuss stays confidential within your care team, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. We’ll go through ten questions covering the past seven days; each one usually takes only a moment to answer.

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin.  
Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I’ve still been able to laugh sometimes—like when my husband made a silly joke yesterday—but it definitely feels harder than it used to. I have to remind myself to lighten up, and even then it doesn’t come as naturally.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Mostly, yes—like I said, I can still laugh, but it takes more effort than before the baby. Sometimes I’ll smile or chuckle, but it fades pretty quickly.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Sometimes… I’ll catch myself looking forward to little things, like my mom bringing over dinner or a quiet moment with coffee, but the bigger stuff—like planning outings—just feels like more work than fun right now.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah, I do that a little. Like if the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle him right away, I’ll think maybe I missed some cue or didn’t feed him properly. It’s not constant, but it pops up a few times a week.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I get that way, mostly at night. My mind races about whether he’s breathing okay or if I’m doing the feedings right—even when everything looks fine. It’s not all day, but it’s hard to shut off once it starts.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky, nothing like that. I mean, I’ll get a tight-chest feeling when I’m lying there wondering if he’s too hot or too cold, but it passes once I check on him.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… some days it feels like the dishes, the laundry, the constant feeding cycle just pile up faster than I can handle. I manage, but by evening I’m wiped out and wondering how I’ll do it all again tomorrow.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say “so unhappy,” but I do have trouble sleeping a few nights a week—mostly because my mind keeps ticking through baby worries or tomorrow’s to-dos. Once I drift off I’m okay, but getting there takes a while.
I have felt sad or miserable
I get waves of that, maybe a few times a week—nothing that lasts all day, but I’ll suddenly feel weepy or heavy, especially when I’m alone with the baby and everything feels quiet and stuck.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t cried like that. I’ve felt teary a couple of evenings, but the tears never actually come—just that tight, thick feeling in my throat for a minute and then it passes.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’m tired and overwhelmed sometimes, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary

Patient-reported symptoms:
- Reduced ability to experience pleasure; laughter requires effort  
- Limited anticipatory enjoyment; only minor events feel rewarding  
- Self-blame when infant is fussy (≈ 2–3×/week)  
- Nocturnal, situation-specific anxiety re: infant safety; occasional chest tightness  
- Episodic low mood/weepiness several evenings per week; tears do not progress to crying spells  
- Sleep-onset difficulty several nights/week linked to racing thoughts  
- Daily tasks feel “on top of” her; reports fatigue and doubts about coping

Patterns:
Mood symptoms mild-moderate, situational, and intermittent; anxiety focused on infant well-being; no anhedonia or pervasive hopelessness; no self-harm ideation.

Screening significance:
Meets partial criteria for **postpartum anxiety**; subthreshold indicators for **postpartum depression** (mood reactivity, fatigue, sleep disturbance, guilt). No current safety concerns.

Risk factors noted:
- Sleep disruption tied to rumination  
- Intermittent guilt/self-criticism  
- Feeling overwhelmed but managing basic tasks

Overall impression:
Elevated distress above typical postpartum adjustment; further clinical evaluation recommended to rule out developing PPD/GAD and to provide supportive interventions.
